themes.theme: Building AI skills and capacity in public administrations
themes.definition: Recommendations to build the skills, roles and internal capacity that public administrations need to develop, buy, use and monitor AI.
themes.what_is_set_out: The 2022 JRC handbook (JRC129100) holds that 'Public institutions need to have civil servants with the right capacities and skills to develop and/or use AI', and that even where national strategies rely on the private sector, government must 'make sure that civil servants can work with the procured AI solutions'. It sees 'a strong need to promote the internal capacity of public administrations' in organisational, structural, human and financial terms to 'develop, experiment, implement and monitor AI', and suggests dedicated capacity-building programmes to give administrations independence from suppliers (coder note), 'train the trainers' schemes for civil servants who commission or build AI, context-specific training modules, and models such as the EU Interoperability Academy, a European master's in AI for public services run by a university consortium, and a proposed federation of business schools and public administration institutes. The 2025 JRC report (JRC143539) says public administrations 'should assess which skills and roles are becoming more relevant', which 'may require' competency-based job profiles, targeted recruitment and continuous training, together with 'a clear understanding of the regulatory framework'. Both are reports with recommendations, mostly without a named holder and with no money attached. Monitoring AI is named as one purpose of internal capacity, but checking outputs is not named as a skill.
themes.holders: Public institutions and public administrations; mostly not stated; national training plans, the EU Interoperability Academy, a university consortium and a proposed federation of schools (mentions or suggestions).
themes.binding: Recommendations and suggestions ('need to', 'could', 'it is suggested', 'should', 'may require'); no consequence stated.
themes.checks: n/a (monitoring AI is named as a purpose of internal capacity, without detail).

quotes.quote: There is a strong need to promote the internal capacity of public administrations in terms of organisational, structural, human and financial resources, to develop, experiment, implement and monitor AI within organisational processes.
developing “train the trainers” schemes within national training plans for civil servants engaged in both the commissioning of and/or direc t development of AI solutions
This may require the development of competency-based job profiles, targeted recruitment, and upskilling and continuous training.
make sure that civil servants can work with the procured AI solutions.

themes.theme: Training and awareness for staff who use or build AI
themes.definition: Training, awareness and literacy programmes that an organisation commits to, or is advised to provide, for its own staff who use, develop or are responsible for AI.
themes.what_is_set_out: The European Court of Auditors will 'introduce a dedicated, compulsory, AI and data-analytics learning programme' for its staff, make sure all staff are trained in responsible use covering data protection, transparency obligations and human oversight requirements, and issue guidelines and hold awareness sessions on ethical concerns. The Commission will identify the skills needed and build a dedicated learning offer, with DG HR mapping upskilling needs by job group, and staff 'will be helped to know how to prompt AI systems to get the most useful results and how to critically assess outputs'; its 2023 staff guidelines already say 'staff must be aware that these models can produce biased and wrong answers'. The European Parliament's 2024 framework is narrower: formal training programmes 'should' be set up for ICT professionals, while awareness for Members, assistants and staff is called 'important' and left to an AI roadmap that 'should' inform end-users. The EDPS says EU institutions 'should train their staff' on generative AI security risks and must make developers aware of data-minimisation techniques, and lists bias, fairness and interpretability training for development teams as a possible measure; ENISA calls for faster awareness and skills 'across all levels of organisations', and EU121 signatories commit to train personnel with Article 50 roles. The programmes differ most in reach (all staff at the ECA, ICT staff in the Parliament) and in whether checking outputs is taught, which is explicit only in the Commission's texts.
themes.holders: The European Court of Auditors; the Commission (AI@EC Network, ISG-AI, DG HR and local HR correspondents); Commission staff (awareness); the European Parliament's administration (holder of training not stated); EU institutions (EDPS texts); organisations generally (ENISA); EU121 signatories.
themes.binding: Institutional commitments ('will') at the ECA and the Commission, with the ECA programme compulsory for staff; an internal rule for Commission staff awareness ('must'); 'should' in the Parliament and EDPS texts (the EDPS uses 'must ensure' for data-minimisation awareness); possible measures in the EDPS risk guidance; ENISA is advisory; EU121 'will make proportionate efforts'. No consequence is stated anywhere.
themes.checks: Output review as a taught skill (AIatEC, EC 2023): trigger: every use (coder note: Rule 2 asks for critical assessment of every response); compared against: not stated; metric or threshold: not stated; who: individual staff users; what happens with the result: not stated.

themes.definition: Specialist roles and in-house expertise that organisations must recruit, keep or develop in order to build, examine and secure AI.
themes.what_is_set_out: The European Parliament's 2024 framework says AI-related profiles such as data scientists, AI architects and engineers 'must be recruited' so that the administration has 'the right level of knowledge, control and oversight', and its 2020 guidelines say the administration 'should remain capable of analysing the evidence used by an AI algorithm and examine the means by which the algorithm produced its answers', while permitting exploratory work 'to build expertise'. The Commission will 'define and recruit the specialist profiles needed to develop AI tools inside the administration'. The EDPS says that because attacks change, 'proper access to advanced knowledge and expertise must be ensured', and suggests diverse teams of data scientists, domain experts and stakeholders to give 'multiple perspectives' on training data and model outputs. ENISA recommends that national authorities 'Develop evaluation capacities' for products with AI functions to 'ensure and validate security levels'. The Parliament's 2020 text is the clearest statement in the cell that a public body should keep the in-house ability to examine how an output was produced.
themes.holders: The European Parliament's administration (the recruiter is not named in the 2024 text); the Commission; EU institutions as controllers (EDPS; holder not stated); national authorities (ENISA).
themes.binding: 'must' in the Parliament's 2024 internal framework and in the EDPS security passage (as interpretation); 'should' in the Parliament's 2020 guidelines; 'will' in AI@EC; a possible measure in the EDPS risk guidance; a recommendation from ENISA. No consequence is stated.
themes.checks: Examining outputs (EP2020): trigger: not stated; compared against: the evidence used by the algorithm and the means by which it produced its answers or actions; metric or threshold: not stated; who: the Parliament's administration; what happens with the result: not stated. Security evaluation (ENISA): compared against 'security levels'; metric not stated; who: national authorities; result not stated.

Develop evaluation capacities for products including AI-functionalities, in order to ensure and validate security levels to face cybersecurity threats

themes.theme: Data protection officers as an advisory resource
themes.definition: The data protection officer as a source of independent advice on AI systems that process personal data.
themes.what_is_set_out: The EDPS says it is important that data protection officers 'advise and assist in an independent manner' and 'have a proper understanding of the lifecycle of the generative AI system', which, per coder note, requires that they receive information on when and how systems process personal data. The EDPB (EU074) lists, among the elements supervisory authorities may consider, 'any advice or feedback provided by the Data Protection Officer' when assessing a claim that a model is anonymous, and 'whether the controller has involved the DPO' when assessing reliance on legitimate interest. The DPO is presented as an existing role that should be informed and involved, not as a new resource.
themes.holders: Data protection officers; the EU institution or controller that must inform and involve them (nearest actor).
themes.binding: Non-binding interpretation ('it is important to ensure'); in EU074 DPO involvement is an element supervisors may weigh, with no stated consequence.
themes.checks: Trigger: when a supervisory authority assesses an anonymity or legitimate-interest claim (EU074). Compared against: not stated. Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: the supervisory authority, drawing on the DPO's advice. What happens with the result: not stated.

quotes.quote: it is important to ensure that DPOs, within their role, advise and assist in an independent manner on the application of the Regulation, have a proper understanding of the lifecycle of the generative AI system
an element to be considered is whether the controller has involved the DPO, where applicable.
any advice or feedback provided by the Data Protection Officer (“DPO”) (where a DPO was - or should have been - appointed)

themes.theme: Internal competence centres, support networks and staff guidance
themes.definition: Internal units, networks, services and guidance through which EU institutions support their own staff in AI projects and use.
themes.what_is_set_out: The European Parliament set up a Centre of Excellence for AI in its administration (2020), describing internal expertise as necessary for responsible development (coder note), and its 2024 framework says the centre 'shall be reinforced into a Competence Centre' within ICT services that ensures services 'receive technical guidance in conducting AI-related projects', with a role to propose, support and guide rather than decide (coder note); its ICT services 'will develop control and assurance mechanisms' to support the framework's principles, in a text that the coder note records as awaiting Bureau approval. The Commission tasks the ISG-AI, the AI@EC Network, the Cloud Centre of Excellence and the Central Intellectual Property Service with giving staff 'access to AI relevant information, advice and help', will issue 'thematic guidelines for staff' for selecting, acquiring, developing, testing and deploying AI, and tells staff they 'may always contact' the IP service for legal advice. The Parliament's 2020 guidelines present themselves as advice on mitigating AI risks. The passages say who gives support, not what the control and assurance mechanisms or the testing guidelines contain.
themes.holders: The Parliament's Centre of Excellence and Competence Centre and its ICT services; the Parliament's Directorate-General for Innovation and Technological Support (2020 guidelines); the Commission's ISG-AI, AI@EC Network, Cloud Centre of Excellence, DIGIT and corporate governance boards, and Central Intellectual Property Service.
themes.binding: Internal rules and commitments ('shall', 'will'), some still at proposal stage; no consequence stated.
themes.checks: Not stated: the Parliament's control and assurance mechanisms and the Commission's guidelines for testing are named, but their trigger, comparator, metric, holder and use of results are not given in these passages.

quotes.quote: The Competence Centre shall ensure that Parliament's services receive technical guidance in conducting AI-related projects.
to support staff and services by providing access to AI relevant information, advice and help.
thematic guidelines for staff, to be applied for the selection, acquisition, development, testing and deployment of AI solutions
For legal advice on intellectual property, Commission staff may always contact the Commission’s Central Intellectual Property Service – EC-IPR@ec.europa.eu

themes.theme: AI tools, licences and infrastructure for staff
themes.definition: AI tools, licences, prompt libraries, reusable components and computing infrastructure provided to staff or to public bodies.
themes.what_is_set_out: The European Court of Auditors will 'acquire sufficient licences to provide all staff with access to at least one general-purpose AI tool', consider on-site models for confidential work, build 'a dedicated library of prompts' for auditors and support services, and consider licences for commercial large language models with API access while addressing data security, confidentiality and compliance. The Commission plans infrastructure and platforms under its dual-pillar approach (with EuroHPC and European data spaces, per coder note), a framework to reuse and contribute to open-source AI, and is investigating corporate conversational platforms able to handle 'sensitive non-classified information'. The 2025 JRC report calls 'Reliable and scalable infrastructure' necessary, with attention to sustainability, and the 2022 handbook points to EU programmes hosting 'AI components that can be freely reused'. The ECA prompt library is the only passage in the cell that treats prompts as a managed, shared resource [inference: it could support consistent use], and no passage links the provision of tools to recording model versions or configurations.
themes.holders: The European Court of Auditors (including its Language and Editorial Directorate); the Commission (ISG-AI, DIGIT, corporate governance boards); commercial model providers (unnamed, in the value chain); EU programmes and EDIHs (reusable components).
themes.binding: Institutional commitments and options ('will', 'will also consider', investigating); recommendations in the JRC reports. No consequence stated.

quotes.quote: the ECA will acquire sufficient licences to provide all staff with access to at least one general-purpose AI tool.
Specific and separate ECA prompt library: we will develop a dedicated library of prompts, tailored to the needs of our auditors and support services.

Introducing multi -purpose conversational platforms for human -like dialogues, using generative AI within the perimeter of the Commission, capable of supporting up to sensitive non-classified information.
Reliable and scalable infrastructure is necessary to support AI adoption and ensure efficiency, flexibility and sustainability.

themes.definition: Requirements, recommendations and provisions on the quality, availability and readiness of the data that public bodies use to build, test and run AI.
themes.what_is_set_out: The European Court of Auditors states that 'Public institutions must ensure that the data they rely on is of good quality' and that it needs 'AI-ready data', to be pursued through data standards and structured data requests (coder note); the Commission aims to strengthen its 'data maturity' as 'the foundation for accurate and effective AI'. The Parliament's 2020 guidelines say: 'Use representative datasets to train and test the AI model.' The JRC reports call for public datasets to be kept open and 'continuously cleansed and updated', for dedicated technical and financial resources for data quality, and for guidance on anonymised datasets (2022), and for 'robust and well-governed data spaces' (2025). ENISA recommends that national authorities 'publish anonymised datasets from Frontier AI simulations' and suggests that public cyber datasets could become a 'European strategic asset' for training and evaluating defensive AI, under strong safeguards. Most of these passages name no provider of the data and attach no resources; representativeness of test data appears only in the Parliament's text.
themes.holders: Public institutions (ECA statement of principle); the ECA itself; the Commission (DIGIT and corporate governance boards); not stated in the Parliament text and most JRC passages; national authorities and European institutions (ENISA); a proposed alliance of universities and research institutions (JRC 2022).
themes.binding: 'must' as a statement of principle (ECA) and as an internal guideline imperative (EP2020); institutional commitments ('we need', 'build on'); recommendations and suggestions in the JRC and ENISA texts. No consequence stated.
themes.checks: Test data (EP2020): trigger: when training and testing a model; compared against: representativeness (of what is not stated); metric or threshold: not stated; who: not stated; what happens with the result: not stated. Otherwise n/a.

quotes.quote: Public institutions must ensure that the data they rely on is of good quality and is governed, processed, and stored in line with EU values, legal frameworks, and strategic interests.

quotes.location: p. 5 (=== page 5), Section III, 'Ethical and Lawf…
quotes.quote: Use representative datasets to train and test the AI model.

There is a need to ensure that non- critical public sector datasets which are developed for specific purposes are not only thematically clustered and kept open, but also continuously cleansed and updated
Access to accurate, reliable and comprehensive data is fundamental for AI solutions to function effectively. Establishing robust and well-governed data spaces is crucial to support AI adoption.

themes.theme: Money: funding programmes, fees and resource allocation
themes.definition: Funding programmes, duties to allocate resources, free access and fees that put money behind AI adoption, testing and compliance.
themes.what_is_set_out: For public-sector adoption, the 2022 JRC handbook points to the Digital Europe Programme and the Recovery and Resilience Facility as including 'funding opportunities dedicated to AI for the public sector', and suggests dedicated quotas in EU programmes for pilots, combining international, national, regional and local funding, earmarked research funding, and money for the quality of public data; the 2025 report points to GenAI4EU funding and calls for 'a stable and adequate allocation' of funding, infrastructure and staff. For testing and compliance, the AI Act asks that sandboxes have 'the adequate resources for their functioning, including financial and human resources' and that Member States ensure authorities 'allocate sufficient resources', makes sandbox access free for SMEs apart from exceptional costs, and reduces conformity-assessment fees for SMEs; the Digital Omnibus has providers pay for testing and assessment when they apply to the Commission. The JRC funding points are opportunities and suggestions rather than allocations. No passage puts money behind checking AI tools that public bodies already use, such as testing, monitoring or human review.
themes.holders: EU programmes (Digital Europe, Recovery and Resilience Facility, GenAI4EU); establishing authorities and Member States (sandbox resources); national competent authorities (free access, cost recovery); fee-setters not named; providers (pay fees under the Omnibus).
themes.binding: Statutory for sandbox resourcing (Art. 57(4)) and for fees; recital 'should'; the JRC texts are descriptions and suggestions ('could', 'it is suggested'). No consequence stated.

quotes.quote: The Digital Europe Programme ,53 as well as the EU Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF)54 programme include funding opportunities dedicated to AI for the public sector.
Establishing authorities should also ensure that the AI regulatory sandboxes have the adequate resources for their functioning, including financial and human resources.

The overarching goal is to ensure a stable and adequate allocation of both economic resources (funding) and non-economic resources (infrastructure, human resources, etc.) to support the development of AI-enabling factors
the GenAI4EU initiative offers funding opportunities to boost EU-made GenAI solutions.

themes.theme: Frameworks, indicators and assistance for assessing AI's impact in public administrations
themes.definition: Frameworks, indicators, data sources and help proposed for public bodies to assess, before and after deployment, what AI does to their services, citizens and values.
themes.what_is_set_out: All passages come from the 2022 JRC handbook. It says 'impact assessment frameworks need to be developed to guide decision -makers and practitioners to introduce AI', proposes 'umbrella' frameworks adapted to countries and sectors with quantitative and qualitative indicators, and says 'Public bodies and agencies need to be assisted when evaluating their AI systems' against intended goals, unintended effects and negative consequences, without naming who would assist. It suggests that a proposed EU observatory share methodologies and indicators, that the forthcoming LORDI indicator framework could be used 'to monitor' that public use of AI is in line with European values and digital principles, and that impact assessments draw on participatory methods and citizen-generated data. It cites existing references: the JRC Code of Conduct for Data Centres for sustainability indicators, adding that this is not enough (coder note), and a Dutch AI impact assessment. These are proposals; none was an available resource when the handbook was written.
themes.holders: Mostly not stated; a proposed EU observatory on AI; the LORDI framework (forthcoming); citizens (data); the JRC and the Dutch ECP Platform (references).
themes.binding: Recommendations and suggestions ('need to be', 'it is suggested', 'could', 'it is recommended'); no consequence stated.
themes.checks: Trigger: ex ante (before introducing AI) and ex post. Compared against: intended goals, unintended effects and potential negative consequences; alignment with European values and digital principles. Metric or threshold: indicators still to be developed; none stated. Who: public bodies, assisted by an unnamed provider. What happens with the result: to guide decisions to introduce AI and what impact to expect [inference from the wording]; otherwise not stated.

quotes.quote: Public bodies and agencies need to be assisted when evaluating their AI systems, whether to assess the achievement of intended goals, to gauge encountered uni ntended effects, or to take stock of potential negative consequences.

impact assessment frameworks need to be developed to guide decision -makers and practitioners to introduce AI in their own organisations, and identify what impact they should expect from their deployment.

Umbrella impact assessment frameworks that would be adapted and contextualised across different countries and sectors, based on key influencing factors, underpinning quantitative as well as qualitative indicators
to monitor that the use of AI -enabled services by public administrations, businesses and citizens be executed in full alignment with European values and digital principles

themes.definition: Ready-made self-assessment lists, checklists and risk-rating methods that organisations can apply to their own AI systems or to their readiness for AI.
themes.what_is_set_out: The 2022 JRC handbook cites the Assessment List for Trustworthy AI (ALTAI), through which 'developers and users of AI can directly assess whether their solution is in line with EU regulations, values and principles'. The EDPS risk guidance offers 'an analytical framework for identifying and treating risks' organised by data protection principles, a risk-rating method in which 'Risk = Likelihood x Impact' on a five-level scale with a risk matrix (described from ISO 31000 rather than prescribed, per coder note), and a checklist mapping each phase of developing or procuring AI to the relevant principles and risks. The coder note records that the checklist lists 'None' for the deployment and retirement phases (the note is cut short, so its full scope is not visible), and that the EDPS says the guidance is not to be relied on as a complete compliance list. The 2025 JRC report offers its enabling factors 'as a baseline for self-assessment' of an administration's readiness. These tools assess risk or readiness, not the accuracy of particular outputs.
themes.holders: ALTAI's provider is not named in the passage (users: developers and users of AI); the EDPS (framework, method, checklist); the JRC report authors (enabling factors).
themes.binding: Offered as voluntary aids; the EDPS method is a description, not a prescribed method; no consequence.
themes.checks: Trigger: each lifecycle phase of development or procurement (EDPS); otherwise whenever the organisation chooses. Compared against: data protection principles (EDPS); EU regulations, values and principles (ALTAI); enabling factors (JRC 2025). Metric or threshold: qualitative levels of likelihood and impact; no acceptance threshold stated. Who: the organisation itself (controller, developer or user). What happens with the result: risk treatment (EDPS); otherwise not stated.

quotes.quote: Through the Assessment List for Trustworthy AI (ALTAI), 86 for example, developers and users of AI can directly assess whether their solution is in line with EU regulations, values and principles
Annex 3: Checklist per phase of the AI lifecycle development
the risk can be evaluated as the product of its likelihood and the severity of its impact (Risk = Likelihood x Impact)

absences: Among the Delivery starting codes, logging and recording have no resource passages at all: nothing provides tools, templates, storage or staff for keeping logs or records of AI use or outputs. Monitoring is thin: the only monitoring resources are the provider's post-market monitoring template (postponed to 2027 and made a 'voluntary template' by the Omnibus) and an indicator framework that the 2022 JRC handbook says is forthcoming; nothing supports a deployer's own monitoring of a tool in use. Validation appears only as a call to identify validation tools (JRC 2022) and as targeted technical access 'for testing and validation' for new providers (Omnibus). Among the Resources starting codes, time is absent: no passage gives reviewers time, and time pressure appears only as a cause of automation bias in EU043 (coder note). Money is present for adoption and for sandboxes but never for testing, monitoring or human review of tools already in use. Outside support exists mainly as powers ('may'), mentions and suggestions. On checking outputs, the passages provide no accuracy thresholds, nothing on the consistency or repeatability of outputs, no confidence scores, no resources for tracking model versions or configurations (the only trace is the coder note that Annex XII information to downstream providers covers versions), prompts only through the ECA prompt library, and no rule on which outputs or cases must reach a human. Public bodies are rarely named as recipients of AI Act resources: only 'local public authorities', 'as appropriate', and the EDPS sandbox for EU institutions; the internal documents of the ECA, the Commission and the Parliament provide resources to their own staff only. Several resources are promised rather than delivered in these passages: the AI Office's FRIA template, joint Commission-EDPB guidance, the post-market monitoring template, national sandboxes (deadline moved to August 2027) and the LORDI indicator framework.
cross_cutting: The cell is dominated by the AI Act's support machinery for providers and small firms (sandboxes, templates, guidelines, help channels, codes of practice, encouraged benchmarks) and by the Act's statutory duties on providers to pass information and access down the supply chain to deployers and downstream providers. A second, separate cluster comes from the EU institutions' own documents (ECA, Commission, Parliament, EDPS), which give their staff training, specialist roles, competence centres, licences and a prompt library, and from two JRC reports that recommend skills, funding and impact-assessment frameworks for public administrations and point to existing EU programmes and facilities, without themselves allocating resources. Binding force is uneven: duties on providers (instructions for use, declared accuracy, access for notified bodies, information for downstream providers) and on deployers (competent, trained and authorised overseers) are statutory, but most resources that public authorities offer are framed as 'may', 'should', 'encourage' or 'could', or are promised for later; the Digital Omnibus softens several (literacy 'support' instead of 'ensure', a voluntary monitoring template, the sandbox deadline a year later) while adding a few duties (literacy support by the Commission and Member States, fines for refusing technical access). The holders are mainly providers, the Commission and AI Office, Member States and national competent authorities, and the EDPS and EDPB; public deployers appear mostly as implied recipients. For checking AI outputs, the main resource is information: providers must declare the accuracy level and metrics against which the system was tested, describe its limits and supply means to interpret its outputs, and the EDPS adds model cards to support regular accuracy checks. The people who check must have competence, training, authority and support, and the Commission plans to help staff 'critically assess outputs'. Benchmarks, however, are only encouraged, the only list of metrics is an EDPS annex without thresholds, explainability and bias tools appear only in footnotes, and nothing provides for consistency or repeatability checks, control of versions or prompts (beyond one prompt library), confidence scores, logging, or deciding which cases reach a human.
